1001186.etyen:
Derived from Latin Antarctica, ultimately from Ancient Greek Ἀνταρκτική (Antarktikḗ), the feminine of ἀνταρκτικός (antarktikós, “opposite the Arctic; southern”), from ἀντ- (ant-, “opposite, against”) + ἀρκτικός (arktikós, “Arctic, northern”). The second element is ultimately from ἄρκτος (árktos, “bear; the Great Bear”), referring to the northern constellations. Doublet of Antarktis (“the Antarctic; Antarctica”).
The name therefore literally denotes the land opposite the Arctic. The modern geographical name was introduced at an Italian scientific congress in 1840 and first appeared on a map in

1001954.etyen:
From Edvard (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Edvard”. The given name Edvard is from English Edward, from Old English Ēadweard, composed of ēad (“wealth, prosperity, fortune”) and weard (“guardian, protector”).
Compare Danish Edvardsen, Swedish Edvardsson and English Edwardson (“patronymic surnames”).
